input: Investigate apprenticeship programs in electrical work

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Knowing whether this is for the user themselves, a family member, or someone else changes the eligibility criteria, tone, and depth of research needed.
Apprenticeship programs are highly location-specific — availability, sponsors, and unions vary dramatically by region or country.

Electrical work covers residential, commercial, and industrial tracks; some programs focus on union (IBEW) paths, others on non-union or trade school routes — knowing which matters changes what to look for.
The applicant's current situation (age, education level, prior experience) may restrict which programs are accessible or how quickly they can start.
Understanding whether the goal is to actually apply now or just gather information determines how actionable and detailed the plan needs to be.
What 'done well' looks like differs greatly — it could mean a shortlist of programs, a completed application, or a comparison of pay and duration.
Some people prioritise earning while learning, others care most about certification type, union membership, or program length — this shapes which options to highlight.

gold.taskDescription: Research available apprenticeship programs in electrical work to evaluate options and determine next steps.

questions.title: Who is this apprenticeship research for?
questions.description: Is this for yourself, a family member, or someone else? This determines eligibility focus and how personal the research should be.

questions.title: What city, state, or country are you based in?
questions.description: Apprenticeship programs are highly regional. Knowing the location narrows down available sponsors, unions, and trade organizations.

questions.title: Are you interested in union, non-union, or either type?
questions.description: Union programs (like IBEW) differ significantly from non-union or independent trade school apprenticeships in structure, pay, and certification.

questions.title: What is the applicant's current education and experience level?
questions.description: Many programs have minimum requirements such as a high school diploma, math prerequisites, or prior trade exposure. This affects which programs are realistic.

questions.title: Is the goal to apply now or just explore options first?
questions.description: Knowing the intended next action determines whether the output should be a general overview or a step-by-step application guide.

questions.title: What does a successful outcome of this research look like?
questions.description: For example: a ranked shortlist of programs, a salary comparison, a single strong recommendation, or a completed application checklist.

questions.title: What matters most — pay, program length, or certification type?
questions.description: Different people prioritise earning potential, how fast they become licensed, union membership, or the specific certification earned. This shapes which programs to highlight.
